sections.h2: Where is the Highland County Recorder in Hillsboro?
sections.html:
The Highland County Recorder works from Suite 108 at 119 Governor Foraker Place in Hillsboro, with mail going to P.O. Box 804, Hillsboro, OH 45133. The county's recorder page gives 937-393-9954 and an 8 to 4 weekday schedule.

Late arrivals get caught by one rule. Anything handed in after 3:30 PM waits overnight and is run the next business day, so a seller racing a closing should be at the counter early in the afternoon at the latest.

The auditor, who has to see your deed first, is at the same street address and answers at 937-393-1915. Hillsboro is the seat of a county of roughly 553 square miles, which means a seller in Greenfield, Lynchburg or a rural township drives in to record.

sections.h2: What does the Highland County Recorder charge per deed?
sections.html:
The recorder's page prints a flat price by page count and marks it as the rates effective January 1, 2025. Two pages or fewer cost $39, and every added page raises the price by $8.

Highland County Recorder price by page count, as printed on the county's page
Length of documentPrice
One or two pages$39
Three pages$47
Five pages$63
Seven pages$79
Ten pages$103

Only cash or a check works for recording. The office takes no credit cards at this time. A marginal notation adds $4 per reference. A UCC form is $12, plus $4 for each name, and only when the filing involves real estate and carries a full legal description.

sections.h2: Which formatting mistakes cost extra in Highland County?
sections.html:
Highland County enforces the Ohio layout rule in section 317.114. A document notarized after July 1, 2009 that ignores it draws a $20 surcharge. Four habits avoid it:

  • Use sheets from 8.5 by 11 up to 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • Print in type of ten points or more, black or blue ink only, with nothing highlighted.
  • Keep a three-inch strip clear on the first page for official stamps.
  • Send a stamped, self-addressed envelope if you want the original mailed back.

The recorder's page also links a county conveyance standards sheet on the auditor's website. Read it before the deed is drafted. A rejection by the tax map office or the auditor costs a second trip even when no money penalty follows.

sections.h2: How does a Highland County deed move between offices?
sections.html:
The county publishes a recording procedure with a set order. First you bring the packet to the Recorder for a quick look at whether it is recordable and the fees are right. Next you visit the Auditor to confirm forms and the conveyance fee. Then you return to the Recorder with payment and contact details.

Behind the counter the packet goes to the Tax Map office, which stamps it or rejects it for fixes. The Auditor checks it again, and the Recorder records it and calls you, or mails it in your envelope. Ask your title company whether it will carry the packet in person.

The auditor's forms page lists the Ohio paperwork: DTE 100 and DTE 100EX for the fee statement and its exemption, DTE 101 for homestead property and DTE 102 for the farm valuation program. The auditor's tools menu also has a conveyance fee calculator that adds a parcel transfer fee. Confirm any figure it produces with the staff.

sections.h2: What do the state statutes add to a Highland County sale?
sections.html:
The auditor endorses the deed after the buyer files a value statement under section 319.202. The seller pays the statement fee in section 319.54(G)(3), which is the larger of $1 or ten cents per $100 of value.

A county can add a transfer tax capped at thirty cents per $100 by section 322.02. The Highland County Auditor knows whether this county has done so. Exemptions cover gifts within a family, deeds for no payment, tax-sale deeds and deeds that only secure a debt.

Farmland needs one more answer on the statement. The county's farm FAQ says land that leaves the valuation program owes a recoupment charge equal to three years of tax savings, so a farm seller should ask the auditor for the figure before signing a contract.

sections.h2: What can a seller look up on the Highland County Auditor's website?
sections.html:
Before you list, spend ten minutes on the auditor's site. These pieces matter most to a seller:

  • A parcel search by number, owner or address, with a GIS viewer for boundaries.
  • A sales report and sales list of recent transfers.
  • A delinquency report for past-due balances.
  • A conveyance fee calculator and a tax estimator.

Those tools answer the questions a buyer's agent will ask. Which nearby parcels changed hands, and for how much? Does the house you are selling show a past-due balance? What would the tax estimator say on the contract price? A seller who has run those lookups can set a price and a closing date without waiting on a title company's search.

The county commissioners meet on Wednesdays at 9:00 AM at Suite 211 of the same building, at 119 Governor Foraker Place, which is where you would go if a road, sewer or planning question affects your lot.

sections.h2: How can Highland County owners watch for deed fraud?
sections.html:
The recorder's page links two guides under the Fraud Sleuth name, one plain and one step by step with pictures. Ask the office how the service works and how to enroll your parcel. That matters most for a vacant, inherited or rented house that nobody checks every day.

Records can be searched through the online records link on the same page, so a seller can pull up the last recorded deed, mortgage or lien before listing. Finding a paid-off mortgage that was never released is better done early than at the closing table. The auditor's site and the recorder's page together cover both the tax side and the title side of a Highland County parcel.

Anyone who inherited a Highland County house should search the parcel before promising a closing date. The last deed on file may be under a relative's name from long ago.

sections.h2: What does the Census say about Highland County homes?
sections.html:
Highland County lies on hilly ground between the Little Miami and Scioto watersheds and was organized in 1805 from parts of Ross, Adams and Clermont Counties. The Census Bureau estimates 43,823 residents in 2025 and 19,196 housing units. Its 2020 to 2024 survey shows owners living in 74.3% of occupied homes, typical home value of $168,900, typical rent of $780 and household income near $65,785.

Fayette, Ross, Pike, Adams, Brown and Clinton Counties share its borders. Buford, Highland Holiday and Rocky Fork Point are census-designated places inside it, all recorded at the same Hillsboro counter.

faqs.q: What does a two-page deed cost to record in Highland County?
faqs.a: $39 under the rates effective January 1, 2025. A three-page deed costs $47, and each added page adds $8 up to $103 at ten pages.

faqs.q: Can I pay the Highland County Recorder by card?
faqs.a: No. The recorder's page says recordings are cash or check only, so bring one of those and a stamped, self-addressed envelope if you want the deed mailed back.

faqs.q: How late can I bring a deed in for same-day recording?
faqs.a: Before 3:30 PM. The office stays open to 4:00 PM, but anything received after 3:30 PM waits for the next business day.

faqs.q: Why is the auditor involved in recording a deed?
faqs.a: Ohio has the auditor review the buyer's value statement and endorse the deed first. In Highland County the packet runs from the recorder to the auditor, the tax map office and back to the recorder.

faqs.q: What if my deed ignores the state layout rules?
faqs.a: The recorder adds $20 for a nonconforming document notarized after July 1, 2009, and the tax map office or auditor may reject it. Black or blue ink and the right margins avoid both.
